source.title: Association of Step Width with Accelerated Sprinting Performance and Ground Reaction Force

paper.citation: Nagahara, R., Mizutani, M., Matsuo, A., Kanehisa, H., & Fukunaga, T. (2017). Association of step width with accelerated sprinting performance and ground reaction force. International Journal of Sports Medicine, 38(7), 534–540. https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0043-106191
paper.abstract: How does step width change across a maximal sprint, and how is it associated with speed and ground-reaction impulses? Seventeen male athletes, age 20.7 ± 1.2 years, 100-m best 11.22 ± 0.28 s. Fastest of two to five 60-m block-start sprints in spikes. Track-sprint context; transfer to football stance, surface, and reactive acceleration is indirect. Cross-sectional GRF and center-of-pressure analysis using 54 force platforms at 1,000 Hz. Step width normalized to stature and averaged into four-step sections through step 22. Many unadjusted section-by-variable correlations were tested.
paper.tldr: This paper informs how step width changes during acceleration and why wider is not a universal technical cue. Step width decreased rapidly through approximately step 13 and then more gradually. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional GRF and center-of-pressure analysis using 54 force platforms at 1,000 Hz. Step width normalized to stature and averaged into four-step sections through step 22. Many unadjusted section-by-variable correlations were tested.
paper.findings: Step width decreased rapidly through approximately step 13 and then more gradually. Normalized step width correlated with running speed only in the 9th–12th-step section (r = 0.507, p = 0.038) among the section analyses. Step width showed strong positive correlations with mediolateral net impulse across all sections (r = 0.801–0.909).
paper.limitations: Small, noninternational-level male sprint sample. Multiple correlations without multiplicity adjustment raise false-positive concern. Correlation does not show that deliberately widening steps improves speed; anatomical range constrains step width. Wider placement may reflect the mechanics that generated the sprint rather than a modifiable independent cause.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat step width as an emergent, phase-specific coordination measure. Avoid blanket “wider” cues; if modifying it, verify changes in sprint time, force direction, and athlete-specific mechanics under the actual football task.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Treat step width as an emergent, phase-specific coordination measure. Avoid blanket “wider” cues; if modifying it, verify changes in sprint time, force direction, and athlete-specific mechanics under the actual football task. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
